chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), so I said, 'When does the food and drink become prohibited for the fasting one, and when does the Dawn Prayer become permissible?' He said, 'When the dawn appears and is like the white Coptic fabric, then the food becomes prohibited, the fast begins, and the Dawn Prayer becomes permissible.' I said, 'So we are not in the time [for eating] until the rays of the sun rise?' He said, 'Far be it! Where are you going? That is the Prayer of the children.'

key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: The dawn, specifically referring to the true dawn marking the start of fasting time
key_terms.الْقُبْطِيَّةُ الْبَيْضَاءُ: The white Coptic fabric, a metaphor for the horizontal band of light indicating true dawn
key_terms.شُعَاعُ الشَّمْسِ: The rays of the sun, referring to the later time when some mistakenly believe fasting begins
key_terms.صَلَاةُ الصِّبْيَانِ: The prayer of the children, referring to the practice of praying early before the true dawn time

ai.seo_question: When does the time for fasting begin according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the precise moment for the prohibition of food and drink during fasting, defining it as the appearance of the white horizontal dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq). It distinguishes this true dawn from the earlier false dawn, which is merely the time for children's practice, thereby establishing the correct time for the Dawn Prayer. This distinction is crucial in Shia jurisprudence for determining the exact start of the daily fast.
